newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lyonnaise sees no surprises for 96 results.
newsitem.headline: Lyonnaise sees no surprises for 96 results.

text.p: French utilities company Lyonnaise des Eaux does not expect any surprises in its 1996 results, deputy chairman Guy de Panafieu said on Friday.
"We do not expect any unpleasant suprise for 1996," he said in an interview with weekly Journal des Finances to appear on Saturday and made available to Reuters.
Chairman Jerome Monod said last September the 1996 profit could see a rise by the same amount as that posted in the first first half, which was 25 percent.
"We are aiming for a return on equity of 10 percent in 1998 and 15 percent in 2000," de Panafieu added.
The company expects to hold the same rate of dividend payments, he said.

"As to the dividend, we maintained it in 1995 despite a disappointing result," he said. "The payout rate, which is already high, will not increase. But if there are big profits, that could allow bigger payments", he added.

The company does not expect to go to the market for funds in the near future and is watching its debt level, which will partly depend on any major acquisitions he said. "But we do not need to go to the market in the near future," he said.
The company's share price has significant potential to rise in 1997, given analysts' conservative estimates of net asset value of more than 600 francs per share, he said.

The current ownership structure suits the company, with Suez -- at 17 percent of the capital -- at a level it has historically held after having fallen to 12 percent when Lyonnaise merged with Dumez, he said.

The newly stabilised and profitable Suez brings "stability and quality" to Lyonnaise' shareholders, which include Axa, with four percent and Credit Agricole, three percent, and other shareholders not on the board.
The company's net debt stands at 20 billion francs and is falling, he said. It should be between 65 and 70 percent of equity by the end of 1996, compared to 73 percent at the end of June.
The company will take a decision on its property provisions when the 1996 accounts are closed and could envisage a provision that took out the rest of its losses, he said.

Lyonnaise has absorbed three billion francs of property losses in the past few years and at the end of 1996 had about 1.5 billion of property stock, on which there were losses of under 200 million. "No bad surprises are expected," he said.
In 1998, the property stock will be under one billion francs and the loss in the year will be less than 100 million, he said.
